# Part I: Repository and Workflow

# Part II: Web Scraping


## Question 1: Scrape a Table


```{r}
# Loading packages used for web scraping and data cleaning per the lectures
library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(janitor)
library(stringr)

```




```{r}
# Reading the Wikipedia page containing Chicago community areas

url <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_areas_in_Chicago"

community_page <- read_html(url)

# Extract all tables from the page and let's inspect them

tables <- community_page %>%
  html_elements("table") %>%
  html_table()

# Display the number of tables found

length(tables)

# we have 5 tables displaying. The likely table we need is #2 with 78 rows 
# and 13 columns

```


```{r}
# Examine the table that contains Chicago community areas

head(tables[[2]])
```



```{r}
# I'm now storing the community areas table and cleaning the column names

community_areas <- tables[[2]] %>%
  clean_names()

# Displaying column names

names(community_areas)

# Displaing dimensions

dim(community_areas)

# All column names match the Wikipedia site :) 

```


```{r}
# Now I display the last rows of the table to locate the citywide total row. Checked
# for the tail command to inspect what is the name of the last row. It's named 
# Chicago

tail(community_areas)
```




```{r}

# I now remove the citywide Chicago total row

community_areas <- community_areas %>%
  filter(name != "Chicago")

# Now I must convert total population from character to numeric value

community_areas <- community_areas %>%
  mutate(
    total_population = as.numeric(
      str_remove_all(total_population, ",")
    )
  )

# Checking there are now 77 community areas

dim(community_areas)

```



```{r}
# Now I want to show the row for West Town

community_areas %>%
  filter(name == "West Town")

# Display the 5 community areas with the largest populations

community_areas %>%
  arrange(desc(total_population)) %>%
  head(5)
```


## Question 2: Scrape with CSS selectors

```{r}

# Reading the Books to Scrape site

books_url <- "https://books.toscrape.com/"

books_page <- read_html(books_url)

```




```{r}

# Extracting  all book containers from the webpage

books <- books_page %>%
  html_elements("article.product_pod")

length(books)
```


```{r}
# Now we have the 20 books, we must extract the title of each book

titles <- books %>%
  html_element("h3 a") %>%
  html_attr("title")

# Let's take a look at the first few titles or the entire list to be sure

head(titles)
titles
```

```{r}
# Extracting the price of each book

prices <- books %>%
  html_element(".price_color") %>%
  html_text2()

# Display first few prices. Matches the prices in the website 

head(prices)
```


```{r}
# Extracting availability information

availability <- books %>%
  html_element(".instock") %>%
  html_text2()

# Display first few availability values. It matches the website
head(availability)
```


```{r}
# Combining the scraped information into a tibble

books_tbl <- tibble(
  title = titles,
  price = prices,
  availability = availability
)

# Display the number of rows

nrow(books_tbl)

# Display the first rows

head(books_tbl)
```




```{r}
# Now I convert price from text (character data) to numeric (numbers)

books_tbl <- books_tbl %>%
  mutate(
    price = as.numeric(str_remove(price, "£"))
  )

# Verifying the change to show numbers only without the currency sign

head(books_tbl)
```



```{r}
# Save the table to a CSV file as required
write.csv(
  books_tbl,
  "books.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```



# Bonus Part: Star Ratings


```{r}
#  BONUS QUESTION: Extract star ratings. The star counts from the website match.

ratings <- books %>%
  html_element(".star-rating") %>%
  html_attr("class")

# Display first few ratings

head(ratings)
```




```{r}
# Convert text ratings into numeric ratings

ratings <- ratings %>%
  str_remove("star-rating ") %>%
  recode(
    "One" = 1,
    "Two" = 2,
    "Three" = 3,
    "Four" = 4,
    "Five" = 5
  ) %>%
  as.numeric()

# Check the first few ratings to make sure we got numbers instead of spelled out
# numbers

head(ratings)
```


```{r}
# Now that it worked finally, I need to add numeric star rating to the books table

books_tbl <- books_tbl %>%
  mutate(star_rating = ratings)

# Display first rows
head(books_tbl)



```






# Part III: Open Data API


## Question 1: Requesting Data


```{r}
# Loading packages for API requests and JSON parsing just like in the lectures

library(httr)
library(jsonlite)
library(dplyr)
```




```{r}

# API endpoint for Chicago 311 service requests. endpoint is the website 

endpoint <- "https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/v6vf-nfxy.json"

# Request the 1,000 most recent West Town requests from 2026 onward

response <- GET(
  endpoint,
  query = list(
    community_area = "24",
    `$where` = "created_date >= '2026-01-01T00:00:00'",
    `$order` = "created_date DESC",
    `$limit` = 1000
  )
)


# Check the response status. Let's hope to get a 200 code. yes !!
status_code(response)
```

##Question 2: Parse response-Convert the JSON response into a data frame


```{r}

# Convert JSON response into the actual data frame

requests_df <- fromJSON(
  rawToChar(response$content)
)


# Display number of rows

nrow(requests_df)

# Display column names

names(requests_df)
```

## QUestion 3:  Summarize Response


```{r}

# Count service requests by type and display the 10 most common ones

top_requests <- requests_df %>%
  count(sr_type, sort = TRUE) %>%
  head(10)

top_requests
```


## Question 4: Interpret the results 

# The 311 service request show that the top request in 2026 was Graffiti removal
# request with 218. Rodent bait came second with 53 and Finance Parking Code Enforcement
# review third with 45. The remaining seven, were relatively closer in request count. 


# I think what the data doesn't show could be problems that people do not report or 
# that are not in the top 1000. 


## BONUS PART: Median completion time



```{r}

# Identify the 5 most common request types
top5_types <- requests_df %>%
  count(sr_type, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice(1:5)

top5_types

```

```{r}
#Store the names of the top 5 requests

top5_names <- top5_types$sr_type

top5_names

```




```{r}
# Now attempting to build the table

bonus_tbl <- requests_df %>%
  filter(status == "Completed") %>%
  mutate(
    created_date = as.Date(created_date),
    closed_date = as.Date(closed_date),
    days_to_close = as.numeric(closed_date - created_date)
  ) %>%
  filter(sr_type %in% top5_names) %>%
  group_by(sr_type) %>%
  summarise(
    median_days = median(days_to_close, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(median_days))

bonus_tbl


```



```{r}
#double checking the request statuses

unique(requests_df$status)
```




# Part IV: Census API



## Step 1: Identify the Variables


```{r}
library(tidycensus)
```


```{r}
# Loading the ACS variable metadata
acs_vars <- load_variables(
  2024,
  "acs5",
  cache = TRUE
)

head(acs_vars)
```




```{r}
acs_vars %>%
  filter(grepl("50.0 percent or more", label))
```




```{r}

# Let's find the Median Household Income. Which one is it though?

acs_vars %>%
  filter(grepl("Median household income", label))
```


```{r}
# Let's find the Median Household Income 
acs_vars %>%
  filter(name == "B19013_001")
```

# Gross Rent as a Percentage of Household Income Total: B25070_001E
# Gross Rent as a Percentage of Household Income 50.0 percent or more: B25070_010E
# Median Household Income: B19013_001E





## Step 2: Retrieve the data




```{r}
# Retrieve ACS data for all Ohio counties as requested
ohio_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  state = "OH",
  variables = c(
    total_renters = "B25070_001",
    severe_rent_burden = "B25070_010",
    median_income = "B19013_001"
  ),
  year = 2024
)

# Display first rows
head(ohio_data)
```

## Step 3: Clean and Transform


## Step 3.1: Create a wide format of the data


```{r}
# Convert from long format to wide format.

library(tidyverse)

ohio_wide <- ohio_data %>%
  select(NAME, variable, estimate) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = variable,
    values_from = estimate
  )

# Display first rows
head(ohio_wide)
```


## Step 3.2: Create Severe Burden Rate

```{r}
# Calculate severe rent burden rate at 50% or more

ohio_wide <- ohio_wide %>%
  mutate(
    severe_burden_rate =
      (severe_rent_burden / total_renters) * 100
  )

# Checking  first rows
head(ohio_wide)
```



## Step 3.3: Arrange counties form highest to lowerst rate



```{r}
# Sort counties by severe rent burden rate
ohio_wide <- ohio_wide %>%
  arrange(desc(severe_burden_rate))

# Display first rows
head(ohio_wide)
```


## BONUS: Split the NAME column into COUNTY and STATE columns



```{r}
# Split NAME into COUNTY and STATE columns. Basically add more columns. 
ohio_wide <- ohio_wide %>%
  separate(
    NAME,
    into = c("county", "state"),
    sep = ", "
  )

# Display first rows
head(ohio_wide)
```
